newsitem.title: ROMANIA: STRIKING ROMANIA MINERS DROP BUCHAREST DEMO PLAN.
newsitem.headline: STRIKING ROMANIA MINERS DROP BUCHAREST DEMO PLAN.

text.p: Striking miners, who sacked the Romanian capital twice in the early 1990s, on Thursday abandoned a plan to descend on the Romanian capital to press pay claims and demands for job security.

About 5,000 miners massed outside coal board offices in the Jiu Valley, 400 km (250 miles) west of Bucharest, unanimously backed a call from trade union leaders to scrap a plan to travel to the capital in a police-escorted convoy of buses.

They agreed instead for union chiefs to meet a government commission to discuss their demands for a 45 percent pay increase and safeguards against job losses under the reformist cabinet's market reforms.
"We have to use our heads and choose the best solution," top negotiator Romeo Beja told the gathering. "It's true that we have reached the end of our tether. But we must keep calm."

Miners had earlier considered sending several thousand miners to Bucharest to voice their grievances. Trade unionists had initially backed the plan but urged rank-and-file members to refrain from any violence.

"You must realise that if we send a couple of thousand miners in Bucharest we will be weak. We could even be beaten by police," Adrian Burlui, another trade unionist, told the rally. "If we stay here, we will be strong."

The Jiu Valley's 45,000 miners, the country's most militant, launched their strike last week and were joined for a time by miners in other regions. But support for their stoppage by other trade unions has been patchy at best.

Thousands of the miners rampaged through Bucharest twice in the early 1990s. They beat up anti-communist protesters in 1990 and attacked government offices a year later when the first post-communist government fell. Seven people were killed.
Miners' head Miron Cosma is on trial charged with leading the 1991 riots in the capital. A court this week rejected his appeal to be released during the proceedings.
A preliminary settlement was reached in talks in Bucharest earlier this week but was torn up by trade union negotiators in the face of rank-and-file anger over the terms.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's centrist government, which took over from ex-communists last November, says the miners will receive the equivalent of a 15 percent pay rise when tax cuts come into effect in August.

Miners take home nearly twice the average Romanian wage. which is equivalent to $80, and still have communist-era benefits like bonuses, cheap electricity and rent. But many say they live and work in intolerable conditions.
Many miners are deeply suspicious of government plans to restructure oversized and loss-making industries and say privatisation would kill off their sector.
Vlad Rosca, Secretary of State responsible for talks with trade unions, hoped the deadlock could be broken.

"Our experience is that negotiations cannot be conducted under pressure," he said by telephone in Bucharest. "Two rounds of talks have produced agreements which were then torn up by the miners who do not appear to recognise their own leaders."
